# 12-Week Resistance Training Programme
### Client Profile & Clinical Context

**Client:** 27-year-old female | **Condition:** PCOS (Rotterdam criteria confirmed)
**Cycle status:** Irregular (35–90 days), intermittently anovulatory — cycle-phase periodisation is not appropriate at this stage
**Endocrinologist directive:** Resistance training as first-line intervention
**Start date:** 1 June 2026 | **Facility:** Full commercial gym
**Programme goal:** Improve insulin sensitivity, support hormonal regulation, build lean mass, improve body composition, and establish sustainable training habits

---

> **Clinical note for trainer:** The evidence base for resistance training in PCOS supports improvements in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), androgen profiles, and menstrual regularity independent of weight loss. Programme design prioritises progressive mechanical load, adequate recovery, and stress management — all of which are relevant to HPA-axis and HPO-axis function in this population. Avoid excessive volume or caloric restriction framing that could compound cortisol burden. If and when cycle regularity improves over the 12 weeks, cycle-phase periodisation can be introduced in a subsequent block.

---

## Programme Architecture at a Glance

| Phase | Weeks | Primary Stimulus | Sessions/Week |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1 — Foundation** | 1–4 | Motor pattern acquisition, connective tissue prep, metabolic baseline | 3 |
| **Phase 2 — Hypertrophy** | 5–8 | Progressive mechanical tension, volume accumulation | 4 |
| **Phase 3 — Strength** | 9–12 | Heavier loading, neural drive, consolidation | 4 |

**Session structure throughout:** Warm-up → Primary compound lifts → Accessory work → Finisher or conditioning → Cool-down/mobility

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION
## Weeks 1–4 | 3 Sessions per Week

### Rationale
The first four weeks serve three purposes simultaneously. First, they allow you to assess the client's true movement quality across all fundamental patterns — squat, hinge, push, pull, carry — before loading becomes meaningful. Second, they begin building the connective tissue resilience (tendons, ligaments, joint capsules) that will be stressed more heavily in Phases 2 and 3. Third, and critically for a PCOS client, they introduce the metabolic stimulus of resistance training in a volume and intensity range that is challenging enough to drive adaptation but not so demanding that it elevates cortisol chronically. Research consistently shows that even moderate-intensity resistance training begins improving insulin sensitivity within two to four weeks, so this phase is not merely preparatory — it is therapeutically active from session one.

Sessions are scheduled Monday, Wednesday, Friday (or any three non-consecutive days the client can commit to). Rest days between sessions are non-negotiable in this phase.

**Phase 1 parameters:**
- Intensity: 60–70% of estimated 1RM (RPE 5–7 out of 10)
- Sets per exercise: 2–3 working sets
- Reps: 10–15
- Rest between sets: 60–90 seconds
- Tempo: Controlled — 3 seconds eccentric, 1-second pause, 1-second concentric (3-1-1) on all compound movements

---

### Week 1 — Orientation and Baseline

**Session A — Lower Body Emphasis**

Begin every session with 8–10 minutes of general warm-up: 5 minutes on the rowing machine at a comfortable pace, followed by the dynamic mobility circuit below. This warm-up is used throughout Phase 1 and should become automatic.

*Phase 1 Dynamic Warm-Up Circuit (perform once through, no rest):*
- Hip circles — 10 each direction
- Bodyweight glute bridge — 15 reps, 2-second hold at top
- World's greatest stretch — 5 each side
- Lateral band walk — 15 steps each direction (light band)
- Goblet squat bodyweight — 10 reps, slow and deliberate
- Dead bug — 8 each side

**Working sets:**

Goblet squat — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Use a dumbbell or kettlebell held at the chest. Focus on heel contact throughout, knees tracking over toes, neutral spine. This is the primary squat pattern assessment tool. Note any valgus collapse, forward lean, or heel rise and address with cues before adding load.

Romanian deadlift (dumbbell) — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Dumbbells allow the client to find her natural hip-width stance without the bar path constraint of a barbell. Hinge at the hip, maintain a long spine, feel the hamstring load before reversing. This is the primary hinge pattern.

Leg press — 2 × 15 @ RPE 5. Bilateral, feet shoulder-width, moderate depth. This is a confidence-builder and allows quad loading without the balance demand of the squat. Use it to gauge lower body strength baseline.

Seated leg curl — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Isolated hamstring work to complement the RDL. Controlled lowering phase is the priority.

Standing calf raise (machine or Smith) — 3 × 15. Full range of motion — full stretch at the bottom, full contraction at the top.

Plank — 3 × 20–30 seconds. Neutral spine, no breath-holding. Progress hold time across the week.

**Session B — Upper Body Emphasis**

*Same warm-up circuit as Session A.*

Seated cable row (neutral grip) — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Initiate with scapular retraction before elbow drive. This teaches the client to feel her back working rather than defaulting to biceps. Pulling movements are prioritised over pushing in this programme because most untrained women present with underdeveloped posterior chain and upper back, and because scapular stability underpins all pressing movements.

Lat pulldown (wide grip, overhand) — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Slight lean back, pull to upper chest, control the return. Pair with the cable row to build vertical and horizontal pull capacity simultaneously.

Dumbbell bench press — 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Flat bench. Feet flat on floor, slight arch in lower back, dumbbells allow natural wrist rotation. Cue: "push the ceiling away, don't just move the weight."

Dumbbell overhead press (seated) — 2 × 12 @ RPE 5. Seated removes the lumbar stability demand while the client is still learning the pattern. Neutral grip or slight pronation, press directly overhead, avoid excessive rib flare.

Dumbbell lateral raise — 3 × 15 @ RPE 5. Light weight, controlled, slight forward lean at the hip. Medial deltoid development supports shoulder health and aesthetics.

Face pull (cable, rope attachment) — 3 × 15 @ RPE 5. External rotation emphasis. This exercise appears in every session of the programme in some form because it directly counteracts the internal rotation pattern that develops from desk work and protects the rotator cuff as pressing loads increase.

Pallof press — 3 × 10 each side. Anti-rotation core stability. Set the cable at chest height, press directly forward, hold 2 seconds, return. This is more functional than crunches and avoids the spinal flexion loading that can be uncomfortable for some clients.

**Session C — Full Body**

*Same warm-up circuit.*

Trap bar deadlift — 3 × 10 @ RPE 6. If the client has shown good hinge mechanics in Session A, introduce the trap bar deadlift here. The neutral grip and more upright torso angle make it more accessible than a conventional barbell deadlift and allow heavier loading sooner. If the trap bar is unavailable, continue with dumbbell RDL.

Bulgarian split squat (bodyweight or light dumbbells) — 3 × 10 each leg @ RPE 6. Rear foot elevated on a bench, front foot far enough forward that the shin remains vertical at the bottom. This is a challenging pattern — use bodyweight only if needed and add load only when the movement is clean. Unilateral work is a cornerstone of this programme because it addresses asymmetries, reduces spinal loading compared to bilateral barbell work, and creates significant metabolic demand.

Push-up — 3 × max reps with good form (or 3 × 10 if capable). Assess whether the client can perform a full push-up. If not, use an incline push-up on a bench. This is a baseline marker — track improvement across the 12 weeks.

Single-arm dumbbell row — 3 × 12 each side @ RPE 6. Knee and hand on bench, neutral spine, row to hip. Unilateral pulling to complement the bilateral cable work.

Dumbbell bicep curl — 2 × 12. Alternating, supinated grip, full range.

Tricep pushdown (cable, rope) — 2 × 12. Elbows fixed at sides, full extension.

Dead bug — 3 × 8 each side. Slow and deliberate. Opposite arm and leg extend simultaneously while lower back stays pressed to the floor.

---

### Weeks 2–4 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 1

The exercise selection remains identical across Weeks 1–4. This is intentional. Repeating the same movements allows the client to develop genuine motor competency and to experience the neurological adaptation that produces rapid early strength gains. Changing exercises too frequently in the foundation phase is one of the most common programming errors — it feels varied but prevents the client from ever getting good at anything.

**Week 2:** Add one working set to all primary compound movements (goblet squat, RDL, trap bar deadlift, cable row, lat pulldown, bench press). Increase load by 2.5–5 kg wherever RPE felt below 6 in Week 1. Plank progresses to 3 × 35–40 seconds.

**Week 3:** Increase load by 2.5–5 kg on all movements where RPE is at or below 7. Reduce reps on compound movements to 10–12 (from 12–15) and increase load accordingly — this is the first small step toward the hypertrophy rep range. Introduce a 10-minute low-intensity finisher on the rowing machine or stationary bike at the end of Session C only (RPE 4–5, conversational pace). This is not cardio for caloric expenditure — it is a mild metabolic stimulus that supports insulin sensitivity without adding cortisol burden.

**Week 4 — Deload within Phase 1:** Reduce volume by approximately 40% (drop one set per exercise, reduce load by 10%). Keep the same movements. This is not a rest week — it is an active recovery week that allows connective tissue to consolidate, the nervous system to recover, and the client to arrive at Phase 2 fresh. For a PCOS client, this deload also serves to prevent the cortisol accumulation that can occur with uninterrupted training stress. Use this week to have a detailed check-in conversation: How is sleep? Energy levels? Any joint discomfort? Mood? These are all relevant clinical data points.

---

---

# PHASE 2 — HYPERTROPHY
## Weeks 5–8 | 4 Sessions per Week

### Rationale
Phase 2 increases both volume and frequency. The fourth session is added, and the programme shifts to an upper/lower split, which allows each muscle group to be trained twice per week — the frequency most strongly supported by the hypertrophy literature. For a PCOS client, building lean mass is directly therapeutic: skeletal muscle is the primary site of insulin-mediated glucose disposal, and each kilogram of additional muscle tissue meaningfully improves insulin sensitivity independent of any change in fat mass.

Intensity increases to 67–77% of 1RM (RPE 7–8). Sets increase to 3–4 working sets per exercise. Reps shift to 8–12 for compound movements and 12–15 for isolation work. Rest periods extend to 90–120 seconds for compound movements and 60–90 seconds for isolation work.

**Session schedule:** Monday (Lower A), Tuesday (Upper A), Thursday (Lower B), Friday (Upper B). Wednesday and the weekend are rest or active recovery days.

---

### Weeks 6–8 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 2

**Week 6:** Increase load by 2.5–5 kg on all barbell movements and 2–4 kg on dumbbell movements where RPE was at or below 7 in Week 5. Add one set to the primary compound movement in each session (barbell squat goes to 5 × 8, bench press goes to 5 × 8, trap bar deadlift goes to 5 × 6–8, overhead press goes to 5 × 8).

**Week 7:** Reduce reps on primary compound movements to 6–8 (from 8) and increase load by 2.5–5 kg. This is a small step toward the strength rep range and prepares the neuromuscular system for Phase 3. Accessory work remains at 10–12 reps. Introduce a 15-minute low-intensity conditioning finisher at the end of Lower B only — rowing machine or stationary bike at RPE 4–5. This is the only cardiovascular component in the programme and is deliberately minimal to avoid cortisol accumulation.

**Week 8 — Deload:** Reduce volume by 40% (drop one set per exercise, reduce load by 10–15%). Keep all four sessions but make them shorter and lighter. This is the second structured deload and is particularly important before the intensity demands of Phase 3. Use this week for a second detailed check-in: strength progress, body composition changes (if the client is tracking), energy, sleep, and any menstrual changes (even small ones — spotting, changes in cycle length — are worth noting and communicating to the endocrinologist).

# PHASE 3 — STRENGTH
## Weeks 9–12 | 4 Sessions per Week

### Rationale
Phase 3 shifts the primary stimulus from hypertrophy to strength. Loads increase to 77–87% of 1RM (RPE 8–9), reps on primary compound movements drop to 3–6, and rest periods extend to 2–3 minutes between heavy sets. Volume on accessory work is maintained to preserve the hypertrophy stimulus. This phase consolidates the lean mass built in Phase 2 and drives meaningful strength gains that will serve as the foundation for any subsequent training block.

For the PCOS client, heavier resistance training has been shown to produce greater improvements in HOMA-IR and testosterone-to-SHBG ratios than moderate-intensity training alone, making this phase clinically important rather than merely performance-oriented. The session split remains upper/lower.

# Nutrition Plan — PCOS & Insulin Sensitivity
### Integrated with 12-Week Resistance Training Programme

---

> **Critical clinical framing for the trainer:** Under-fuelling is not a neutral error in this population — it is actively harmful. Chronic caloric restriction elevates cortisol, suppresses LH pulsatility, worsens HPA-axis dysregulation, and can deepen anovulation in an already irregular cycle. The research is unambiguous: aggressive caloric deficits in women with PCOS worsen the hormonal environment even when weight loss occurs. This nutrition plan is built around **adequate fuelling for training adaptation and hormonal function first**, with body composition improvement as a downstream consequence of improved insulin sensitivity — not the primary lever being pulled.
>
> Do not frame any part of this plan to the client as a weight-loss diet. Frame it as **eating to support her training, her hormones, and her health.**

---

## Nutrition Philosophy for This Client

The core metabolic problem in PCOS-related insulin resistance is impaired glucose disposal — skeletal muscle cells are less responsive to insulin signalling, so the pancreas compensates with higher insulin output. Chronically elevated insulin drives ovarian androgen production (via LH amplification and direct ovarian stimulation), suppresses SHBG, and perpetuates the cycle of irregular ovulation. The nutrition strategy therefore targets three things simultaneously:

**1. Stabilise postprandial glucose and insulin excursions** — through food quality, meal composition, and timing — without restricting total energy intake to a degree that stresses the HPA axis.

**2. Support muscle protein synthesis** — because every kilogram of lean mass added is a kilogram of insulin-sensitive tissue that improves glucose disposal around the clock, not just during exercise.

**3. Reduce systemic inflammation** — which is elevated in PCOS independently of body composition and contributes to both insulin resistance and ovarian dysfunction.

---

## Energy Intake — Establishing the Right Target

### Why a deficit is not the starting point

For a 27-year-old woman with PCOS beginning a resistance training programme, the priority in Weeks 1–8 is eating at or very close to **total daily energy expenditure (TDEE)**. A small, conservative deficit of no more than 10–15% of TDEE may be appropriate from Week 9 onward *only* if the client is progressing well, energy is good, and she explicitly wants to pursue body recomposition. Even then, this is a conversation to have with the endocrinologist in the loop.

### Estimated energy targets

These are starting estimates based on a moderately active 27-year-old female. Adjust based on real-world response over the first two to three weeks — energy levels, training performance, sleep quality, and hunger patterns are all feedback signals.

**Weeks 1–8 (maintenance / slight surplus on training days):**
- **Rest days:** approximately 1,800–2,000 kcal
- **Training days:** approximately 2,000–2,200 kcal
- The training day increase reflects the additional energy cost of resistance training sessions and the elevated protein synthesis demand in the post-exercise window

**Weeks 9–12 (optional conservative deficit if appropriate):**
- **Rest days:** approximately 1,700–1,900 kcal
- **Training days:** approximately 2,000–2,200 kcal (training day intake is never reduced — fuelling the session and recovery is non-negotiable)

> **Practical note:** If the client is currently eating significantly below these numbers — which is common in women with PCOS who have been told to "eat less" — do not jump immediately to the full target. Increase by 100–150 kcal per week over two to three weeks to allow metabolic adaptation and avoid the psychological discomfort of a sudden large increase. This is called a **reverse diet approach** and is appropriate here.

---

## Macronutrient Targets

### Protein — The Non-Negotiable Priority

**Target: 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight per day**

Protein is the highest priority macronutrient in this plan for two reasons. First, it is the direct substrate for muscle protein synthesis — without adequate protein, the resistance training stimulus cannot produce the lean mass gains that drive insulin sensitivity improvement. Second, protein has the highest thermic effect of food (approximately 25–30% of its calories are used in digestion), the strongest satiety signal per calorie, and the most stable effect on postprandial blood glucose of any macronutrient.

For a client weighing approximately 65–75 kg, this translates to roughly **120–165 g of protein per day.** Use the client's actual bodyweight to calculate her specific target.

Protein should be distributed across **four to five eating occasions** throughout the day rather than concentrated in one or two meals. The muscle protein synthesis response to a single protein dose plateaus at approximately 40–50 g in most individuals, so spreading intake maximises the anabolic stimulus across the day.

**High-quality protein sources to prioritise:**
- Chicken breast, turkey breast, lean beef mince (5% fat), sirloin steak
- Salmon, cod, tuna, mackerel, sardines (the oily fish also provide anti-inflammatory omega-3s — a dual benefit)
- Eggs and egg whites (whole eggs are preferred — the yolk contains choline, vitamin D, and fat-soluble nutrients relevant to hormonal function)
- Greek yoghurt (full-fat, plain — see dairy note below)
- Cottage cheese
- Tofu, tempeh, edamame (if plant-based options are preferred)
- Whey protein isolate or concentrate as a supplement when whole food sources are inconvenient — not as a replacement for meals

### Carbohydrates — Quality and Timing Over Restriction

**Target: 35–45% of total daily calories, adjusted by training day**

This is where the most important nuance lies. Carbohydrate restriction is frequently recommended for PCOS and insulin resistance, and while very low carbohydrate diets can improve insulin markers in the short term, they carry significant risks in this population: they can suppress thyroid function, elevate cortisol, impair training performance, reduce muscle glycogen availability (blunting the hypertrophy response), and — critically — they are very difficult to sustain, leading to restriction-rebound cycles that worsen the metabolic picture over time.

The approach here is **carbohydrate quality and strategic timing**, not restriction.

**Carbohydrate quality principles:**

Choose carbohydrates with a low-to-moderate glycaemic index and high fibre content. Fibre slows gastric emptying, blunts the postprandial glucose spike, feeds beneficial gut bacteria (which independently influence insulin sensitivity via short-chain fatty acid production), and increases satiety. Target a minimum of **30–35 g of fibre per day.**

*Prioritised carbohydrate sources:*
- Oats (rolled or steel-cut — not instant) — beta-glucan fibre has specific evidence for improving insulin sensitivity
- Sweet potato, regular potato (cooled after cooking — cooling increases resistant starch content)
- Brown rice, basmati rice (lower GI than other white rices), quinoa
- Lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans — these are dual protein-carbohydrate sources and among the most insulin-friendly foods available
- Whole grain bread and pasta — in moderation, not as the dietary foundation
- All vegetables — non-starchy vegetables (broccoli, spinach, kale, courgette, peppers, cucumber, asparagus) are essentially unlimited and should form the base of every meal
- Berries — blueberries, raspberries, strawberries — low sugar, high in polyphenols with specific evidence for improving insulin signalling
- Apples, pears, oranges — whole fruit with the fibre intact, not juiced

*Carbohydrate sources to minimise (not eliminate — this is not a prohibition):*
- Ultra-processed foods with refined flour and added sugar
- Sugary drinks including fruit juice, energy drinks, and sweetened coffee drinks
- White bread, white pasta, and white rice as dietary staples (occasional consumption is not a problem)
- Breakfast cereals with high sugar content

**Carbohydrate timing — the most important practical tool:**

Distribute the majority of carbohydrate intake around training sessions. This is called **nutrient timing** and it serves two purposes: it ensures muscle glycogen is available for training performance, and it exploits the post-exercise window during which skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity is dramatically elevated — meaning carbohydrates consumed in the two hours after resistance training are preferentially directed to muscle glycogen replenishment rather than fat storage, and do so with a lower insulin response than the same carbohydrates consumed at rest.

- **Pre-training (60–90 minutes before session):** 30–50 g of moderate-GI carbohydrate with 20–30 g of protein. This fuels the session without causing a large insulin spike immediately before exercise.
- **Post-training (within 60 minutes of finishing):** 40–60 g of carbohydrate with 30–40 g of protein. This is the highest-priority meal of the day. Do not skip it.
- **Rest day carbohydrate distribution:** Spread evenly across meals, with slightly lower total intake than training days. Do not drop carbohydrates dramatically on rest days — this creates unnecessary metabolic stress.

### Fat — Hormonal Function and Anti-Inflammation

**Target: 25–35% of total daily calories**

Dietary fat is essential for steroid hormone synthesis — all sex hormones, including oestrogen and progesterone, are synthesised from cholesterol. Very low fat diets impair hormonal function. Fat also slows gastric emptying, which blunts postprandial glucose excursions when consumed alongside carbohydrates.

**Fat quality is the priority:**

*Prioritised fat sources:*
- Extra virgin olive oil — the most evidence-supported dietary fat for insulin sensitivity and inflammation reduction. Use as the primary cooking fat and for dressings.
- Avocado and avocado oil
- Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, anchovies) — omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) have direct evidence for reducing ovarian inflammation and improving insulin receptor sensitivity in PCOS
- Walnuts, almonds, Brazil nuts, cashews — also provide magnesium (see micronutrients below)
- Flaxseed and chia seeds — plant-based omega-3 (ALA) and lignans which may support oestrogen metabolism
- Whole eggs
- Full-fat plain Greek yoghurt and full-fat dairy in moderation

*Fats to minimise:*
- Refined seed oils (sunflower, corn, soybean, vegetable oil) used in ultra-processed foods — high omega-6 content promotes the inflammatory pathway
- Trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) — found in some processed baked goods and fast food — directly worsen insulin resistance
- Excessive saturated fat from processed meat sources (bacon, sausages, deli meats daily)

## Meal Structure — The Practical Framework

### The Plate Model (every main meal)

Rather than asking the client to count macros obsessively — which can increase cortisol and create an unhealthy relationship with food — teach her the following plate structure as a default template. Macro tracking can be used for the first two to three weeks to calibrate portion sizes, then relaxed into this intuitive framework.

**Half the plate:** Non-starchy vegetables. Broccoli, spinach, mixed salad leaves, roasted courgette, peppers, asparagus, green beans, cauliflower. These provide fibre, micronutrients, and volume with minimal glucose impact.

**One quarter of the plate:** Quality protein source. A palm-sized portion of chicken, fish, beef, eggs, tofu, or legumes.

**One quarter of the plate:** Quality carbohydrate source. A fist-sized portion of sweet potato, rice, oats, lentils, or whole grain.

**A thumb-sized portion of fat:** Olive oil drizzled over the vegetables, half an avocado, a small handful of nuts, or the fat naturally present in the protein source (salmon, eggs).

This structure automatically produces a balanced macronutrient profile, a high fibre intake, and a moderate glycaemic load at each meal without requiring the client to calculate anything.

### Meal Frequency and Timing

**Four meals per day** is the recommended structure for this client. Three meals plus one targeted post-workout meal or snack. This frequency maintains a steady amino acid supply for muscle protein synthesis, prevents the large glucose excursions that come with infrequent large meals, and avoids the prolonged fasting periods that can elevate cortisol in susceptible individuals.

Skipping breakfast is not recommended for this client. There is specific evidence in PCOS populations that front-loading calories earlier in the day (larger breakfast, moderate lunch, smaller dinner) improves insulin sensitivity and LH:FSH ratios compared to the reverse pattern. This does not need to be rigid, but the client should be discouraged from the common pattern of skipping breakfast, eating a small lunch, and consuming the majority of calories in the evening.

**Sample daily meal timing (training day, morning session):**

- **7:00 am — Pre-training meal:** Oats with protein powder stirred in, topped with berries and a tablespoon of almond butter. Or two scrambled eggs on whole grain toast with half an avocado.
- **9:30 am — Training session**
- **11:00 am — Post-training meal (priority meal):** Greek yoghurt with berries and granola, plus a chicken and rice bowl. Or a protein shake with a banana immediately post-session, followed by a full meal within the hour.
- **1:30 pm — Lunch:** Large salad with salmon, quinoa, roasted vegetables, olive oil and lemon dressing.
- **6:30 pm — Dinner:** Lean beef stir-fry with broccoli, peppers, and brown rice. Or baked cod with sweet potato and green beans.

**Sample daily meal timing (rest day):**

- **8:00 am — Breakfast:** Three-egg omelette with spinach, mushrooms, and feta. Whole grain toast. Coffee or tea.
- **12:30 pm — Lunch:** Lentil and vegetable soup with a small whole grain roll. Or a large chicken and vegetable bowl with hummus.
- **4:00 pm — Snack (if hungry):** Apple with almond butter. Or cottage cheese with cucumber and a small handful of walnuts.
- **7:00 pm — Dinner:** Grilled salmon with roasted sweet potato, asparagus, and a drizzle of olive oil.

## Micronutrients — The PCOS-Specific Priorities

Several micronutrients have specific evidence in PCOS and insulin resistance and are commonly deficient in this population. These should be addressed through food first, with supplementation as a targeted adjunct where dietary intake is insufficient.

### Magnesium
Magnesium is a cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions, including insulin receptor signalling. Deficiency is extremely common in insulin-resistant individuals and is associated with worsened glucose metabolism. Women with PCOS have been shown to have lower serum magnesium than controls.

**Food sources:** Dark leafy greens (spinach, kale), pumpkin seeds, almonds, dark chocolate (70%+), black beans, avocado, whole grains.

**Supplementation:** If dietary intake is insufficient, magnesium glycinate or magnesium citrate at 200–400 mg per day in the evening is well-tolerated and has the added benefit of supporting sleep quality — which is independently important for insulin sensitivity and cortisol regulation. Advise the client to discuss supplementation with her endocrinologist before starting.

### Vitamin D
Vitamin D deficiency is present in the majority of women with PCOS and is independently associated with insulin resistance, impaired follicular development, and worsened androgen profiles. It functions as a steroid hormone precursor and has receptors in ovarian tissue.

**Food sources:** Oily fish, egg yolks, fortified dairy. Dietary sources alone are rarely sufficient, particularly in northern latitudes or for individuals with limited sun exposure.

**Supplementation:** 1,000–2,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily is a reasonable starting point, but the endocrinologist should check serum 25-OH vitamin D and dose accordingly. Pair with vitamin K2 (100 mcg) to support calcium metabolism.

### Inositol (Myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol)
This is worth raising with the endocrinologist specifically. Myo-inositol is a naturally occurring compound involved in insulin signal transduction, and it has the strongest evidence base of any nutritional supplement in PCOS — multiple randomised controlled trials show improvements in insulin sensitivity, ovarian function, and menstrual regularity. The typical evidence-based dose is 4 g of myo-inositol daily (often combined with 400 mcg of folic acid). This is not a recommendation to supplement without medical oversight, but it is a conversation worth initiating with the endocrinologist given the strength of the evidence.

**Food sources:** Citrus fruits, cantaloupe, beans, whole grains, nuts — but dietary amounts are far below the therapeutic doses used in research.

### Omega-3 Fatty Acids (EPA and DHA)
As noted in the fat section, omega-3s have direct anti-inflammatory effects relevant to PCOS. If the client is not eating oily fish at least three times per week, a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 2–3 g of combined EPA and DHA daily is appropriate. Look for a product that has been third-party tested for heavy metals.

### Iron
Women with irregular or heavy periods are at risk of iron deficiency, which impairs training performance and energy levels. If the client reports fatigue disproportionate to her training load, request that the endocrinologist check serum ferritin (not just haemoglobin — ferritin is a more sensitive marker of iron stores). Dietary iron from red meat, lentils, spinach, and fortified foods should be emphasised, and vitamin C-rich foods consumed alongside plant-based iron sources to enhance absorption.

### Zinc
Zinc is involved in insulin synthesis and secretion, and zinc deficiency is associated with worsened insulin resistance. It also plays a role in androgen metabolism. Food sources include red meat, shellfish (oysters are exceptionally high), pumpkin seeds, and legumes.

---

## Hydration

**Target: 2.5–3 litres of total fluid per day**, increasing on training days and in hot weather.

Adequate hydration is directly relevant to insulin sensitivity — even mild dehydration impairs glucose metabolism and increases cortisol. Water should be the primary fluid. Coffee and tea (unsweetened) count toward fluid intake and are not contraindicated — moderate caffeine consumption (up to 200–300 mg per day, roughly two to three cups of coffee) does not worsen insulin resistance in most individuals and may modestly improve it. However, caffeine consumed within six hours of sleep onset impairs sleep quality, which worsens insulin sensitivity the following day — so afternoon and evening caffeine should be avoided.

Alcohol should be minimised. It directly impairs insulin signalling, disrupts sleep architecture, and provides empty calories that displace nutrient-dense food. This is not a prohibition, but the client should understand the mechanism so she can make informed choices.

---

## Foods with Specific Evidence in PCOS — Worth Emphasising

The following foods have direct mechanistic or clinical evidence for benefit in PCOS and insulin resistance and should be actively encouraged rather than merely permitted:

**Cinnamon:** Has been shown in small RCTs to improve insulin sensitivity and reduce fasting glucose in PCOS. Add to oats, yoghurt, smoothies, or coffee. Aim for half to one teaspoon daily. Ceylon cinnamon is preferred over Cassia for regular use.

**Apple cider vinegar:** One to two tablespoons diluted in water before a carbohydrate-containing meal has been shown to blunt postprandial glucose spikes by slowing gastric emptying. Always diluted — undiluted ACV damages tooth enamel. This is a simple, low-cost tool.

**Berries:** Blueberries in particular have evidence for improving insulin receptor sensitivity via polyphenol pathways. Include daily.

**Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale):** Contain indole-3-carbinol and DIM (diindolylmethane), which support oestrogen metabolism via the liver. Relevant to the oestrogen-progesterone balance in PCOS.

**Spearmint tea:** Two cups per day has been shown in RCTs to reduce free testosterone in PCOS via anti-androgenic mechanisms. This is a simple, pleasant, and evidence-based addition. Worth recommending explicitly.

**Fermented foods (plain yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut):** Support gut microbiome diversity, which is increasingly linked to insulin sensitivity and systemic inflammation. Include at least one serving daily.

---

## What to Avoid Framing as "Bad Foods"

This is a coaching note as much as a nutrition note. Women with PCOS have frequently been told by well-meaning clinicians and online sources that they must avoid carbohydrates, dairy, gluten, and a long list of other foods. This creates food anxiety, orthorexic tendencies, and restriction-rebound cycles — all of which worsen the stress response and hormonal environment.

The framework here is **addition before subtraction.** Focus conversations on what the client is adding to her diet — more protein, more vegetables, more fibre, more omega-3s, more water — rather than what she is removing. When the diet is full of high-quality food, there is naturally less room for low-quality food, and this happens without the psychological burden of prohibition.

Occasional pizza, chocolate, a glass of wine, or a restaurant meal does not derail a 12-week programme. Chronic under-fuelling, chronic stress about food, and chronic restriction do.

---

## Weekly Nutrition Check-In Protocol

At each weekly training session, spend five minutes on the following questions. Keep brief notes.

- Energy levels during training and throughout the day (1–10)
- Sleep quality (hours and subjective quality)
- Hunger levels — is she eating enough? Feeling satisfied?
- Any digestive changes (relevant to fibre increases)
- Any menstrual changes, however small
- Mood and stress levels

These data points allow you to adjust the nutrition plan responsively. If energy is consistently low, increase carbohydrate intake on training days. If the client reports feeling bloated, review fibre sources and increase water intake. If sleep is poor, review evening caffeine and consider magnesium supplementation discussion with the endocrinologist.

# Cardio Integration — PCOS & Insulin Sensitivity
### Addendum to 12-Week Resistance Training Programme

---

> **Clinical framing for the trainer:** Cardio prescription in PCOS requires more care than in a general population client. The evidence supports moderate-intensity cardiovascular exercise as an independent improver of insulin sensitivity, VO2 max, and cardiovascular risk markers — all of which are elevated concerns in PCOS. However, high-intensity or high-volume cardio chronically elevates cortisol, can suppress ovarian function further, and competes with recovery from resistance training. The word "moderate" in this prescription is clinically meaningful, not a vague descriptor. It means specific intensity zones, specific durations, and specific placement within the weekly schedule that protects rather than undermines the primary resistance training stimulus.

---

## Cardio Philosophy for This Client

Two cardio sessions per week is the right dose for this client at this stage. Not three, not four. The resistance training programme is the primary therapeutic and adaptive stimulus — the cardio is additive, not competitive. Every cardio session is therefore designed with three constraints in mind:

**Intensity must stay moderate.** This means Zone 2 to low Zone 3 in heart rate zone terminology — a pace at which the client can speak in full sentences but is breathing noticeably. This is approximately 60–75% of maximum heart rate. Above this threshold, the cortisol response increases meaningfully and recovery from resistance training is compromised. Below it, the cardiovascular and metabolic stimulus is insufficient to drive adaptation.

**Duration is capped.** Thirty to forty-five minutes per session in Phases 1 and 2, extending to forty-five minutes maximum in Phase 3. Longer sessions at moderate intensity are not more beneficial for this client — they simply accumulate more cortisol and fatigue without proportional return.

**Placement within the week is deliberate.** Cardio sessions are never placed the day before a heavy resistance training session. They sit on days that create maximum buffer between the resistance sessions they follow and precede.

---

## Heart Rate Zones — Establishing the Client's Targets

Before the first cardio session, establish the client's maximum heart rate. The most accurate method is a graded exercise test, but a practical field estimate is acceptable at this stage: **220 minus age = estimated maximum heart rate.** For a 27-year-old client, this gives an estimated maximum of 193 beats per minute.

| Zone | % of Max HR | BPM (estimated, 27-year-old) | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zone 1 | 50–60% | 97–116 | Very light — warm-up, cool-down, active recovery |
| **Zone 2** | **60–70%** | **116–135** | **Light-moderate — primary cardio target, Phases 1–2** |
| **Low Zone 3** | **70–75%** | **135–145** | **Moderate — upper cardio target, Phase 3** |
| Zone 3 | 75–80% | 145–154 | Moderate-hard — avoid for sustained periods |
| Zone 4–5 | 80–100% | 154–193 | Hard to maximal — not prescribed in this programme |

A heart rate monitor or fitness tracker worn during cardio sessions is strongly recommended. Without objective heart rate data, clients almost universally either underestimate or overestimate their intensity. For this client, drifting into Zone 4 during what she perceives as moderate effort is a real risk, particularly on equipment like the treadmill where pace can creep upward unnoticed.

The **talk test** is a useful backup check: if she cannot comfortably speak a full sentence, she is above the target zone and should reduce intensity immediately.

---

## Equipment Selection and Rationale

Two cardio modalities are prescribed, rotating across the week. This rotation serves two purposes: it prevents the repetitive stress injuries that come from performing the same movement pattern repeatedly, and it provides slightly different metabolic and muscular stimuli that complement the resistance training programme.

**Primary modality: Rowing machine**
The rowing machine is the preferred cardio tool for this client for several reasons. It is a full-body movement that engages the posterior chain — the same musculature being developed in the resistance programme — meaning it reinforces rather than conflicts with the training adaptations being built. It is low-impact, placing no compressive load on the knees or hips. It has a high caloric cost per unit of time at moderate intensity compared to walking or cycling. And it requires enough technique engagement to keep the client mentally present rather than disengaged. Technique cues for the rower: drive with the legs first, then lean back slightly, then pull the handle to the lower chest — the sequence is legs, body, arms on the drive and arms, body, legs on the recovery. Damper setting should be 4–5 for most clients (this is not a drag race — a lower damper setting at higher stroke rate is more cardiovascularly demanding than a high damper setting at low stroke rate).

**Secondary modality: Stationary bike (upright or recumbent)**
The stationary bike is the secondary modality, used on the second cardio day of each week. It is purely lower body, which means it does not add upper body fatigue on top of the pressing and pulling work from resistance sessions. It is the most joint-friendly option available and allows very precise intensity control. Resistance should be set so that the client is working at the target heart rate at a cadence of 80–100 RPM — this is a cycling cadence, not a slow grind. A low cadence with high resistance is not the target; it becomes more like leg press than cardio and the cardiovascular stimulus is lost.

**Tertiary option (outdoor or treadmill walking with incline):**
On weeks where the gym is inaccessible, or as an occasional substitute, brisk walking at a 4–6% incline on a treadmill or hilly outdoor terrain is an acceptable alternative. This must be genuinely brisk — heart rate should reach Zone 2 (116–135 BPM) and stay there. Flat leisurely walking does not meet the threshold. Outdoor walking has the added benefit of natural light exposure, which supports circadian rhythm regulation and cortisol patterning — a genuine secondary benefit for this client.

---

## Weekly Schedule Integration — All Three Phases

The cardio sessions slot into the existing weekly structure as follows. The resistance training sessions are shown for context.

### Phase 1 Schedule (Weeks 1–4) — 3 Resistance + 2 Cardio

| Day | Session | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Resistance — Session A (Lower) | Primary training day |
| Tuesday | **Cardio — Rowing machine, 30 min** | 24 hours after resistance; Zone 2 |
| Wednesday | Resistance — Session B (Upper) | Fully recovered from Tuesday cardio |
| Thursday | **Cardio — Stationary bike, 30 min** | 24 hours after resistance; Zone 2 |
| Friday | Resistance — Session C (Full Body) | Fully recovered from Thursday cardio |
| Saturday | Active recovery or complete rest | See active recovery section below |
| Sunday | Complete rest | |

The Tuesday and Thursday cardio sessions are placed the day after resistance sessions, not the day before. This is deliberate. Performing cardio the day before a heavy resistance session impairs muscle glycogen availability and increases perceived exertion during the lifts. Performing it the day after means the resistance session has already taken priority, and the cardio serves as a mild active recovery stimulus that increases blood flow to worked muscles and supports glycogen replenishment when paired with adequate carbohydrate intake.

### Phase 2 Schedule (Weeks 5–8) — 4 Resistance + 2 Cardio

| Day | Session | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Resistance — Lower A | Primary training day |
| Tuesday | Resistance — Upper A | |
| Wednesday | **Cardio — Rowing machine, 35–40 min** | Recovery day between resistance pairs; Zone 2 |
| Thursday | Resistance — Lower B | Fully recovered from Wednesday cardio |
| Friday | Resistance — Upper B | |
| Saturday | **Cardio — Stationary bike, 35–40 min** | Weekend; Zone 2 to low Zone 3 |
| Sunday | Complete rest | |

In Phase 2, the four-day resistance split means the cardio sessions must be placed more carefully. Wednesday sits naturally between the Monday-Tuesday and Thursday-Friday resistance pairs — it is the only day in the working week where cardio does not immediately precede a resistance session. Saturday cardio follows Friday's Upper B session with at least 24 hours of buffer and precedes a full rest day on Sunday, meaning the client arrives at Monday's Lower A session fully recovered.

### Phase 3 Schedule (Weeks 9–12) — 4 Resistance + 2 Cardio

| Day | Session | Notes |

| Monday | Resistance — Lower A (Squat focus) | Heavy session — fully rested |
| Tuesday | Resistance — Upper A (Bench focus) | |
| Wednesday | **Cardio — Rowing machine, 40–45 min** | Zone 2 to low Zone 3; active recovery |
| Thursday | Resistance — Lower B (Deadlift focus) | Heaviest session of the week |
| Friday | Resistance — Upper B (OHP focus) | |
| Saturday | **Cardio — Stationary bike, 40–45 min** | Zone 2; pre-rest day placement |
| Sunday | Complete rest | Non-negotiable in Phase 3 |

In Phase 3, Thursday's deadlift session is the most neurally and physically demanding session of the entire programme. It is critical that Wednesday's cardio session does not compromise it. Wednesday cardio must therefore stay firmly in Zone 2 — not creeping into Zone 3 — and the client should consume her full training-day nutrition on Wednesday even though it is a cardio-only day. The deadlift session on Thursday takes priority over everything else in the schedule.

## Session Structure — Every Cardio Session

Each cardio session follows the same three-part structure regardless of modality or phase.

### Part 1 — Warm-Up (5 minutes)
Start at Zone 1 intensity — very easy, conversational, heart rate below 116 BPM. On the rower, this means a slow, deliberate stroke rate of 18–20 strokes per minute with minimal resistance. On the bike, a light resistance at 80 RPM. This is not optional — cold cardiovascular tissue and unprepared joints should not be taken immediately to working intensity. Use this five minutes to also mentally settle into the session.

### Part 2 — Steady-State Working Interval (20–35 minutes, progressing across phases)
Bring heart rate up to the target zone and maintain it there for the duration. The goal is **steady state** — a consistent heart rate, not intervals, not surges, not racing. If heart rate drifts above the upper target (135 BPM in Phases 1–2, 145 BPM in Phase 3), reduce intensity immediately. If it stays below the lower target (116 BPM), increase intensity slightly. Check heart rate every five minutes and adjust as needed.

The working interval duration progresses as follows:

- **Weeks 1–2:** 20 minutes
- **Weeks 3–4:** 25 minutes
- **Weeks 5–6:** 30 minutes
- **Weeks 7–8:** 35 minutes
- **Weeks 9–10:** 40 minutes
- **Weeks 11–12:** 45 minutes (Saturday session only — Wednesday stays at 40 minutes to protect Thursday's deadlift)

This progression is gradual and intentional. Adding five minutes every two weeks allows cardiovascular adaptation without the sudden volume jump that would stress the recovery system.

### Part 3 — Cool-Down (5 minutes)
Return to Zone 1 intensity for five minutes, then stop. Do not step off the machine and immediately sit down — keep moving at very low intensity to allow heart rate to return toward resting gradually. Follow with five minutes of static stretching targeting the hip flexors, hamstrings, calves, and thoracic spine. This cool-down period is also an opportunity for the client to practise diaphragmatic breathing — slow, deep breaths in through the nose and out through the mouth — which activates the parasympathetic nervous system and begins the cortisol clearance process.

---

## Intensity Monitoring — Practical Tools

**Heart rate monitor:** A chest strap monitor (Polar H10 or equivalent) is the most accurate option. Wrist-based optical monitors on fitness trackers are acceptable but can read 5–10 BPM high or low during exercise, so the client should be aware of this margin of error.

**Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE):** Use the Borg CR10 scale as a backup. Target RPE of 4–5 out of 10 for Zone 2 work ("somewhat hard" — breathing is elevated but comfortable, could hold a conversation). RPE 5–6 for low Zone 3 work in Phase 3 ("hard" — breathing is clearly elevated, sentences are possible but require effort).

**Talk test check-ins:** Every ten minutes during the working interval, the trainer (if present) or the client herself should attempt to say a full sentence aloud. If she cannot complete it comfortably, intensity is too high.

---

## Nutrition Around Cardio Sessions

Cardio sessions are not fasted. This is a firm recommendation for this client. Fasted cardio is frequently promoted for fat loss but in a PCOS population it elevates cortisol, can cause hypoglycaemic symptoms in insulin-resistant individuals, and provides no meaningful metabolic advantage over fed-state moderate cardio. The stress response to fasted exercise is the opposite of what this client's hormonal environment needs.

**Pre-cardio (30–60 minutes before):**
A small, easily digestible meal or snack containing 20–30 g of carbohydrate and 15–20 g of protein. This does not need to be a full meal — it is a fuelling snack. Examples:

- Greek yoghurt with a small banana
- A slice of whole grain toast with peanut butter and half a banana
- A small bowl of oats with a scoop of protein powder
- A protein shake with a piece of fruit

**Post-cardio (within 45–60 minutes):**
A full meal following the plate model described in the nutrition plan. On cardio-only days (Wednesday and Saturday), this meal should still include a meaningful carbohydrate portion — 40–50 g — because the cardio session has drawn on muscle glycogen and that glycogen needs to be replenished to support the next resistance session. Do not treat cardio days as low-carbohydrate days.

**Hydration during cardio:**
Sip water throughout the session — approximately 150–200 ml every 15 minutes. For sessions over 40 minutes in Phase 3, a small amount of electrolytes (sodium, potassium) can be added to the water via a low-sugar electrolyte tablet or a pinch of sea salt with a squeeze of lemon. This is not necessary for shorter sessions.

---

## What This Cardio Prescription Is Not

Given how much conflicting advice exists around cardio and PCOS, it is worth being explicit about what is not being prescribed here and why.

**Not HIIT.** High-intensity interval training produces a significantly larger cortisol response than steady-state moderate cardio, and the evidence for HIIT superiority over moderate continuous training in PCOS specifically is not strong enough to justify the recovery cost in a client who is simultaneously running a progressive resistance programme. HIIT may be introduced in a subsequent training block once the client's hormonal environment has stabilised and her training age is higher. Not now.

**Not daily cardio.** Two sessions per week is the evidence-informed dose. More is not better. The marginal benefit of a third cardio session is outweighed by the additional recovery demand and cortisol accumulation, particularly in Phase 3 when resistance training intensity is at its highest.

**Not fasted.** As above — fasted cardio is contraindicated for this client.

**Not used as caloric compensation.** The client should not be told that she "earned" extra food through cardio, nor that she needs to "burn off" anything. Cardio is a health and adaptation tool, not a punishment or a transaction. This framing matters for the client's relationship with both exercise and food.

**Not a weight-loss tool.** The cardio prescription is designed to improve cardiovascular fitness, insulin sensitivity, and recovery — not to create a caloric deficit. If the client asks whether the cardio will help her lose weight, the honest and clinically appropriate answer is: it will improve your metabolic health, which over time supports healthy body composition, but we are not using it to burn calories and we are not reducing your food intake to compensate for it.

---

## Active Recovery — The Third Weekly Movement Component

In addition to the two structured cardio sessions, encourage the client to incorporate one active recovery session per week on a rest day — typically Saturday in Phase 1 or Sunday in Phases 2 and 3. This is not a training session. It is deliberate low-intensity movement designed to increase parasympathetic tone, reduce muscle soreness, and support psychological wellbeing.

Appropriate active recovery options:

**Walking:** 20–40 minutes outdoors at a genuinely easy pace. Natural light exposure is a bonus. Heart rate should stay in Zone 1 — below 116 BPM. If she is breathing hard, she is walking too fast.

**Yoga or mobility flow:** 20–30 minutes of gentle yoga, focusing on hip flexors, hamstrings, thoracic spine, and shoulders — the areas most loaded by the resistance programme. Yoga Nidra or restorative yoga specifically has evidence for reducing cortisol and improving HRV (heart rate variability), which is a marker of autonomic nervous system recovery.

**Swimming:** Easy laps at a comfortable pace. Excellent for active recovery because the hydrostatic pressure of water reduces muscle soreness and the horizontal position reduces cardiovascular demand at a given effort level.

**What active recovery is not:** It is not a bonus cardio session. It is not a HIIT class. It is not a spin class. If the client is tempted to use the active recovery slot for additional intense exercise, this is worth exploring in conversation — it may indicate an unhealthy relationship with exercise or anxiety about rest days, both of which are worth addressing directly and compassionately.

## Monitoring and Red Flags

Track the following at each weekly check-in and adjust the cardio prescription if any red flags appear:

**Reduce cardio intensity or duration if:**
- Resting heart rate increases by more than 5–7 BPM above the client's established baseline (a reliable marker of accumulated fatigue or overreaching)
- Training performance in resistance sessions declines for two consecutive weeks without a clear explanation

- Energy levels are stable or improving

# Clinical Adjustment — Late June Flare
### Targeted Recovery Week Modification

---

> **Note to trainer:** This adjustment covers the affected week only. Everything before and after it stands as written. The adjustment is designed to work within the existing programme architecture — it does not shift subsequent weeks, change phase boundaries, or alter the long-term progression. You are absorbing the flare within the programme rather than rebuilding around it.

---

## Identifying the Affected Week

The programme starts 1 June 2026. A heavy flare reported in late June places it within **Week 4 (approximately 22–28 June 2026).**

This is, by design, the Phase 1 deload week — the 40% volume reduction week that was already built into the programme for recovery and consolidation. This is genuinely fortunate timing. The deload week's reduced volume and intensity give you a legitimate clinical framework to work within. However, a standard deload is not sufficient here. Lower-back inflammation and pain require specific modifications that go beyond simply dropping a set per exercise.

**Do not attempt to compensate for this week in Week 5.** The flare is not lost training time that needs to be recovered — it is a physiological event that needs to be respected. Week 5 begins Phase 2 exactly as written.

---

## What the Flare Tells You Clinically

A four-day heavy flare with lower-back inflammation in a PCOS client warrants a brief clinical pause before adjusting the programme. Lower-back pain and pelvic inflammation can occur in PCOS for several reasons — prostaglandin-driven inflammation, referred pain from pelvic congestion, or musculoskeletal pain amplified by the systemic inflammatory state that accompanies insulin resistance. It can also be coincidental musculoskeletal pain from the new training stimulus. You are not diagnosing — but you are making programming decisions that need to account for the possibility that the lumbar spine and surrounding soft tissue are genuinely irritated, not merely sore.

The guiding principle for this week is: **load the system enough to maintain the neural adaptations from Weeks 1–3, protect the lower back completely from compressive and shear forces, and use the week to actively support recovery rather than simply doing less of the same thing.**

---

## Week 4 — Modified Flare Recovery Week
### 22–28 June 2026

**Session frequency:** Reduce from three sessions to two sessions this week. The third session is replaced entirely with active recovery. Do not attempt to fit three sessions into a week where the client is managing active inflammation and pain.

**Lower back rule for the entire week:** No spinal loading. This means no barbell or dumbbell movements where the lumbar spine is under compressive load in a flexed or hinged position. No Romanian deadlifts, no trap bar deadlifts, no bent-over rows, no good mornings. No exercises performed standing where the lower back must stabilise against meaningful load. This is a firm boundary for this week, not a suggestion.

**Pain as a guide:** If any exercise produces pain — not discomfort, not muscle fatigue, but pain — stop that exercise immediately. Modify or substitute. The client should understand this distinction clearly before the session begins.

---

### Session 1 — Upper Body Only, Seated and Supported
**Day:** Monday 22 June (or first available day after the acute flare has passed — if she is still in active pain on Monday, push this session to Tuesday or Wednesday without guilt)

**Duration:** 35–40 minutes maximum. This is shorter than a standard Phase 1 session. Fatigue management is part of the prescription this week.

*Warm-up (5 minutes):*
Seated arm circles — 10 each direction. Seated thoracic rotation with hands behind head — 10 each side. Band pull-apart — 15 reps. Seated cat-cow (hands on knees, gentle spinal flexion and extension only to the point of comfort) — 8 reps. No lower body warm-up elements this session.

**Working sets:**

Seated cable row (neutral grip) — 2 × 12 @ RPE 5. Reduce load by 20% from Week 3. Seated position removes all lumbar demand. Initiate with scapular retraction, keep the torso completely upright — no forward lean or backward drive that would load the lower back.

Lat pulldown (wide grip) — 2 × 12 @ RPE 5. Seated, controlled. Same load reduction. Pull to upper chest, avoid any arching of the lower back at the bottom of the movement.

Seated dumbbell overhead press — 2 × 10 @ RPE 5. Seated with back support if available (use an adjustable bench set to 90 degrees). The back support removes the lumbar stability demand entirely. Reduce load by 15–20% from Week 3.

Dumbbell lateral raise — 2 × 12 @ RPE 4. Light weight. Seated if standing causes any lower back discomfort.

Face pull (cable, rope) — 2 × 15 @ RPE 4. Maintain this. It requires no lower back involvement and supports the postural work that will be important when full training resumes.

Seated dumbbell bicep curl — 2 × 12. Light weight, seated.

Tricep pushdown (cable, rope) — 2 × 12. Standing is fine here as the load is minimal and the torso remains upright.

**No core work this session.** Standard core exercises — planks, dead bugs, Pallof press — all require lumbar stabilisation under load. With active lower-back inflammation, this is contraindicated. The core will be reintroduced carefully in Session 2 if pain has reduced.

---

### Session 2 — Lower Body, Unloaded and Horizontal Where Possible
**Day:** Thursday 25 June (minimum 48 hours after Session 1; if Session 1 was pushed to Wednesday, move this to Friday or Saturday)

**Rationale for including lower body work:** Avoiding the lower body entirely for a week is tempting but counterproductive. The glutes, hamstrings, and quads can be trained without loading the lumbar spine if exercise selection is careful. Maintaining lower body neural activation also supports blood flow to the pelvic region, which may assist with inflammation resolution. The key is horizontal and supine positioning where the spine is supported by the floor or a bench, and unloaded standing movements where the lumbar spine is not under compressive force.

*Warm-up (5 minutes):*
Supine — lying on the back. Knee-to-chest stretch — hold 30 seconds each side, gentle. Supine piriformis stretch (figure-four) — hold 30 seconds each side. Glute bridge — 10 reps, bodyweight only, 2-second hold at top. Lateral band walk — 10 steps each direction, light band, only if standing is comfortable. If standing causes lower back pain, skip the lateral band walk.

**Working sets:**

Glute bridge (barbell or bodyweight) — 3 × 15, bodyweight only this week. Supine position, feet flat on the floor, drive through the heels, squeeze the glutes at the top. The lumbar spine is supported by the floor throughout. This is the primary glute exercise for the week and replaces the hip thrust, which requires the upper back on a bench and creates a different spinal position that may be uncomfortable during a flare.

Leg press — 3 × 15 @ RPE 5. Reduce load by 20% from Week 3. The leg press is appropriate here because the back is fully supported by the machine pad throughout the movement. Feet shoulder-width, moderate depth. Avoid pressing to full knee extension with a snap — controlled throughout.

Seated leg curl — 3 × 12 @ RPE 5. Seated position, back supported. Reduce load by 15% from Week 3. This maintains hamstring activation without any spinal loading.

Seated leg extension — 2 × 15 @ RPE 4. Introduce the leg extension this week as a supported quad exercise. This would not normally feature prominently in this programme, but it is the safest quad isolation option when standing and hinging movements are contraindicated. Light weight, full range of motion, controlled lowering.

Seated calf raise (machine) or standing calf raise at very light load — 3 × 15. If standing calf raises cause any lower back discomfort due to the upright loaded position, switch to seated calf raises on the machine.

**Core — modified, pain-dependent:**
If lower back pain has meaningfully reduced by this session (not absent, but reduced), introduce one gentle core exercise only:

Supine heel slide — 3 × 10 each side. Lying on the back, knees bent, feet flat. Slowly slide one heel along the floor until the leg is nearly straight, then return. This activates the deep stabilisers (transversus abdominis, multifidus) without any spinal flexion or extension load. It is a rehabilitation-grade exercise and is appropriate here precisely because of that.

If pain has not reduced, skip core work entirely and add an extra set of glute bridges instead.

**No session 3 this week.** The Friday full-body session that would normally close out Week 4 is cancelled. Replace it with the active recovery session described below.

### Active Recovery — Replacing Session 3
**Day:** Saturday 27 June (or Sunday 28 June)

This is not a training session. It is a deliberate therapeutic movement session designed to support inflammation resolution, maintain parasympathetic tone, and keep the client feeling connected to her programme during a difficult week.

**Duration:** 20–30 minutes total. No more.

**Option A — Gentle yoga or mobility flow (preferred):**
Focus entirely on the hips, glutes, and thoracic spine. Avoid any deep forward folds, spinal twists under load, or poses that compress the lumbar spine. Appropriate poses and movements include:

- Child's pose — hold 60 seconds, focus on breathing into the lower back
- Supine figure-four stretch — 60 seconds each side
- Supine knee-to-chest — 30 seconds each side
- Cat-cow on hands and knees — 10 slow repetitions, only to the range that is comfortable
- Seated thoracic rotation — 10 each side
- Legs up the wall (Viparita Karani) — 5 minutes at the end. This is a restorative yoga posture where the client lies on her back with her legs resting vertically against a wall. It reduces lower limb oedema, activates the parasympathetic nervous system, and requires zero lumbar effort. It is one of the most genuinely restorative things she can do this week.

**Option B — Gentle walking:**
20 minutes at a very easy pace on flat ground. Zone 1 only — heart rate below 116 BPM. No incline this week. Walking on flat terrain with a natural gait does not significantly load the lumbar spine and the rhythmic movement supports blood flow and mood. If walking causes pain, stop and choose Option A instead.

**Option C — Swimming or pool walking:**
If the client has access to a pool, gentle swimming or walking in chest-deep water is an excellent option. The hydrostatic pressure reduces inflammation, the horizontal swimming position unloads the spine, and the water resistance provides gentle full-body movement without impact. Backstroke or gentle freestyle only — no butterfly or breaststroke, which can hyperextend the lumbar spine.

## Nutrition Adjustments for the Flare Week

The nutrition plan does not require major restructuring, but three specific adjustments support inflammation resolution during this week.

**Increase omega-3 intake.** If the client is not already supplementing with fish oil, this week is the time to start (with endocrinologist awareness). Increase oily fish consumption to daily if possible — salmon, mackerel, or sardines at lunch or dinner. EPA and DHA have direct prostaglandin-modulating effects that are relevant to the inflammatory component of this flare.

**Increase anti-inflammatory foods actively.** Turmeric with black pepper (the piperine in black pepper increases curcumin bioavailability by up to 2,000%) added to meals, smoothies, or warm drinks. Ginger — fresh or ground — in cooking or as a tea. Tart cherry juice (100–200 ml, unsweetened) has specific evidence for reducing inflammatory markers and muscle soreness and is worth adding this week. Blueberries daily.

**Maintain caloric intake.** There is a temptation — the client's and sometimes the trainer's — to reduce food intake during a week of reduced training. Resist this. The body's inflammatory and repair processes are energetically expensive. Reducing calories during active inflammation slows tissue repair, impairs immune function, and increases cortisol. Maintain the full training-day caloric target on Session 1 and Session 2 days. On the active recovery day and any complete rest days, maintain the rest-day target (1,800–2,000 kcal) — do not drop below it.

**Magnesium.** If the client is not already taking magnesium glycinate, this week is a reasonable time to introduce it (with endocrinologist sign-off). 300–400 mg in the evening supports muscle relaxation, reduces prostaglandin-driven cramping, and improves sleep quality — all directly relevant to a flare week.

**Hydration.** Increase to the upper end of the target — 3 litres minimum this week. Adequate hydration supports synovial fluid production, reduces inflammatory mediator concentration in tissues, and supports renal clearance of inflammatory byproducts.

## Communication and Expectation Management

Have a direct conversation with the client at the start of this week. The following points are worth covering explicitly:

**This week is part of the programme, not a deviation from it.** The deload was already planned. The flare has modified it, but it has not derailed anything. Week 5 begins Phase 2 on schedule.

# Flare Management Protocol — Ongoing
### For an Irregular, Unpredictable Cycle in PCOS

---

> **Framing note for the trainer:** This is not a reactive document — it is a standing operating procedure. Because this client's cycle cannot be predicted, you cannot plan around flares in advance the way you would with a regular cycle. What you can do is build a decision-making framework that you and the client both understand clearly, so that when a flare arrives — and it will — neither of you is improvising under pressure or making conservative decisions out of anxiety. The goal is to respond proportionately, protect long-term progress, and avoid the two failure modes that are equally damaging: training through pain that warrants rest, and resting through discomfort that warrants modified training.

---

## The Core Problem

Cycle-phase periodisation — adjusting training load based on the follicular and luteal phases — is a legitimate and increasingly evidence-supported approach for women with regular cycles. It works because the hormonal environment is predictable: oestrogen peaks around ovulation, progesterone dominates the luteal phase, and training tolerance, recovery capacity, and injury risk shift in knowable ways across the cycle.

This client does not have that predictability. Her cycle runs 35–90 days with intermittent anovulation, meaning she may not have a luteal phase at all in some cycles. She cannot tell you on Monday that her period is due Friday. A flare can arrive with a day's warning or none. Attempting to apply standard cycle-phase periodisation to this client right now would create more anxiety and scheduling disruption than benefit.

The framework below therefore does not attempt to predict. It responds. It gives you a tiered, consistent, clinically grounded response to flares of any severity, at any point in the training programme, without requiring you to know where she is in her cycle.

---

## Step One — Establish the Client's Flare Baseline

Before you can respond proportionately to a flare, you need to know what this client's flares actually look like. The late June flare gives you one data point. You need more. From this point forward, ask the client to track the following in a simple notes app, journal, or shared document — whatever she will actually use consistently.

**What to track at every flare:**

- **Date it started and date it ended** — duration matters for programming decisions
- **Pain location** — lower back, pelvic, abdominal, referred down the legs, or a combination
- **Pain intensity** — use a simple 1–10 scale, where 1 is barely noticeable and 10 is incapacitating
- **Associated symptoms** — heavy bleeding, clotting, nausea, fatigue, bloating, mood changes, sleep disruption
- **What made it better** — heat, rest, movement, medication, nothing
- **What made it worse** — sitting, standing, exercise, specific movements
- **Training impact** — was she able to train at all? Modified? Full session?
- **Recovery time** — how many days until she felt able to train normally again

After three to four flares, patterns will emerge. Some clients find their flares are consistently two to three days of high pain followed by rapid resolution. Others have a longer tail of low-grade discomfort that lingers for a week. Some find that movement helps; others find it worsens symptoms acutely. This individual pattern data is more useful than any general protocol, and it allows you to make increasingly accurate programming decisions over time.

Share this tracking data with the endocrinologist at every appointment. It is clinically valuable information that may influence medical management decisions.

---

## Step Two — The Flare Severity Classification

Not all flares are equal and they should not all receive the same training response. The following three-tier classification gives you a consistent language for assessing each flare and a clear corresponding action for each tier. Assess the client at the start of any session where a flare is reported or suspected.

---

### Tier 1 — Mild Flare
**Characteristics:** Pain present but manageable, rated 1–4 out of 10. No significant lower back inflammation. Fatigue is mild. The client can move normally, sit and stand without difficulty, and reports that she feels capable of doing something in the gym even if not a full session. Bleeding may be present but is not heavy enough to cause significant discomfort or anaemia symptoms.

**Training response:** Modify, do not cancel. The session happens but with specific adjustments.

Remove all spinal loading — no barbell squats, deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts, or overhead press from a standing position. Replace with supported and horizontal alternatives as described in the exercise substitution library below. Reduce working weight by 10–15% across all remaining exercises. Reduce total sets by one per exercise. Keep rep ranges the same. Rest periods can extend by 30 seconds if needed — there is no rush.

Cardio for the week: maintain the scheduled sessions but reduce intensity to Zone 1–2 only and cap duration at 20–25 minutes regardless of which phase of the programme she is in. If the stationary bike causes pelvic discomfort due to the seat pressure, switch to the rowing machine or walking.

The client should leave a Tier 1 session feeling that she did something meaningful but is not depleted. If she leaves feeling worse than when she arrived, the session was too much.

---

### Tier 2 — Moderate Flare
**Characteristics:** Pain rated 5–7 out of 10. Meaningful lower back or pelvic inflammation. Fatigue is significant — the client reports that normal daily activities feel effortful. Sleep may have been disrupted. Bleeding is heavy. She can move but with discomfort, and certain positions or movements are clearly painful.

**Training response:** Significantly modified session or active recovery only, depending on the day within the flare.

**Days 1–2 of a Tier 2 flare:** No structured resistance training. Replace the scheduled session with the active recovery protocol (gentle yoga, flat walking, or pool movement as described in the June flare adjustment). This is not optional and should not be negotiated. Training through the acute peak of a Tier 2 flare elevates cortisol, worsens systemic inflammation, and does not produce meaningful training adaptation because the physiological environment is not conducive to it. The client is not losing fitness. She is managing a medical symptom.

**Days 3–4 of a Tier 2 flare (if pain is reducing):** Introduce a modified session using only the Tier 1 substitution library — supported, horizontal, unloaded movements. Assess pain response during the warm-up. If pain increases during warm-up, stop and return to active recovery for another day.

**Days 5+ of a Tier 2 flare:** If the flare is still at Tier 2 intensity after five days, this warrants contact with the endocrinologist before resuming any structured training. A prolonged moderate flare may indicate something that needs medical attention rather than a modified training programme.

Cardio for the week: cancel both scheduled cardio sessions. Replace with active recovery movement only — gentle walking or yoga. Reintroduce cardio in the first full week after the flare resolves, starting at 20 minutes Zone 2 regardless of which phase of the programme she is in, then returning to the scheduled progression the following week.

---

### Tier 3 — Severe Flare
**Characteristics:** Pain rated 8–10 out of 10. The client is significantly incapacitated — unable to perform normal daily activities comfortably, possibly bedridden for part of the day. Severe lower back inflammation. Possibly accompanied by nausea, vomiting, or syncope. Extremely heavy bleeding with large clots.

**Training response:** Complete rest. No gym. No active recovery session. No walking programme.

This is a medical event, not a training variable. The trainer's role in a Tier 3 flare is to communicate clearly that rest is the correct and prescribed response — not a failure, not laziness, not lost progress — and to encourage the client to contact her endocrinologist or GP if the severity is beyond what she has experienced before or if she has any concern about the bleeding volume.

Return to training after a Tier 3 flare follows the same clearance check used after the June flare: pain resolved or minimal, sleep adequate, energy normal, no active pelvic pain. Add one additional criterion for Tier 3: the client should feel genuinely ready to train, not merely willing to push through. The distinction matters.

When returning after a Tier 3 flare, treat the first week back as a mini-deload regardless of where it falls in the programme. Reduce volume by 30–40%, reduce load by 15–20%, and rebuild over the following week before returning to the scheduled progression. Do not attempt to compress missed sessions into the return week.

## The Exercise Substitution Library

This is a standing reference — a pre-built list of substitutions for every major movement pattern that can be applied immediately when a flare requires removing spinal loading. Having this list prepared means you are not improvising exercise selection while the client is standing in front of you in pain.

| Trap bar deadlift | Glute bridge + seated leg curl | Replaces the compound stimulus with two isolation movements |

| Ab wheel rollout | Omit entirely during flare | Too much lumbar extension demand |
